title: How Is AI Changing Supply Chain Operations?
summary: Learn how AI in supply chain operations improves visibility, automates workflows, optimizes transportation and warehousing, and delivers measurable business results.
body_text: Key takeaways AI delivers value when embedded directly into supply chain operations, not when used as a standalone tool. Logistics AI solutions improve efficiency across transportation, warehousing, and fleet management. Supply chain optimization AI drives measurable gains in cost reduction, service, and visibility. Scalable AI adoption requires strong governance, trusted data, and enterprise-wide integration. AI is rapidly becoming a core part of modern supply chain operations. Companies are moving beyond experimentation and applying AI to solve everyday challenges across transportation, warehousing, fleet management, and customer service. From predicting disruptions before they happen to automating workflows and improving real-time decision-making, AI is helping supply chains operate faster, smarter, and with greater precision. As adoption accelerates, scaling it correctly to fit your operations remains a challenge. According to Gartner, organizations will abandon up to 60% of AI projects through 2026 due to a lack of AI-ready data. In supply chain operations, the impact is even more pronounced because AI initiatives often depend on fragmented transportation systems, inconsistent warehouse data, and disconnected fleet platforms. Many AI supply chain initiatives never move beyond pilot stages because they are not connected to core operations. Insights remain isolated, and teams are left with more data but no clear way to act on it. Instead of improving performance, these efforts often introduce complexity and slow down decision-making. Real progress comes from embedding AI directly into supply chain operations, where intelligence becomes part of daily workflows across transportation, warehousing, and fleet management. When applied correctly, AI supports faster decisions, automates routine processes, and drives measurable improvements in cost, service, and visibility. Ryder’s approach reflects that philosophy by integrating AI across its platforms that delivers consistent, scalable outcomes. Continue reading to learn how AI in supply chain operations moves from visibility to action, scales across the network, and delivers measurable results through real-world use cases. From Visibility to Action: Turning Supply Chain Data Into Real-Time Decisions Supply chains generate vast amounts of data every day, yet access to information alone does not improve performance. The real challenge lies in turning that data into timely decisions that can influence outcomes while operations are still in motion. Many systems focus on reporting, which leaves teams reacting after disruptions have already occurred. Ryder applies real-time supply chain optimization AI to support decision-making directly within operational workflows. Instead of relying on static reports, teams are equipped with insights that guide actions as conditions change. Key capabilities include: Faster decision-making : AI highlights critical signals and presents clear recommendations in real time, enabling teams to respond without having to navigate multiple systems. Decisions that once required hours of analysis can now be made in minutes, improving responsiveness across logistics operations . Automated workflows : Routine processes are handled through AI-driven optimization and predefined intelligence rules that trigger actions automatically. This reduces manual effort while ensuring consistency in execution. Real-time issue resolution : Disruptions are identified as they occur, enabling teams to take corrective action immediately. Alerts and recommended responses help resolve issues before they escalate, improving service reliability. Greater alignment between data and action allows operations to run more efficiently, with fewer delays and more consistent performance across the supply chain. Intelligence at Scale: Driving Consistent Performance Across the Supply Chain Meaningful impact requires intelligence to operate across the entire supply chain rather than within isolated functions. Individual use cases can deliver improvements, but consistent performance comes from connecting those insights across systems, teams, and workflows. Ryder embeds AI across its core solutions so intelligence flows seamlessly between transportation, warehousing, and fleet operations. This creates alignment between planning, execution, and delivery outcomes while reducing fragmentation. AI is deployed across: Fleet Management Solutions (FMS) : AI fleet management solutions improve vehicle utilization, monitor performance, and anticipate maintenance needs, helping reduce downtime and increase asset efficiency. Supply Chain Solutions (SCS) : AI enhances visibility and streamlines workflows across warehousing and distribution, enabling faster responses to operational changes. Dedicated Transportation Solutions (DTS) : AI-enabled transportation management improves route planning, delivery accuracy, and real-time adjustments, strengthening reliability while controlling costs. When intelligence operates at scale, improvements in one area reinforce performance across the network, creating a more connected and efficient supply chain. Real Use Cases, Not Theory Practical application defines the value of AI in supply chain operations. Rather than focusing on abstract capabilities, Ryder prioritizes use cases that improve execution, accuracy, and efficiency across daily workflows. Key applications include: #1. AI-powered ETA and arrival tracking AI-driven arrivals and departures continuously refine estimated delivery times using real-time data, improving accuracy and strengthening coordination between operations and customers. #2. Route optimization and backhaul matching AI route optimization software evaluates traffic conditions, demand patterns, and constraints to determine efficient routes. Backhaul matching reduces empty miles and improves asset utilization, with machine learning models driving utilization gains. #3. Automated case summarization and routing AI agents streamline high-volume communication workflows by summarizing cases and routing them to the appropriate teams, reducing response times and improving operational efficiency. #4. Intelligent document processing (invoices, POs, contracts) Intelligent document processing standardizes and extracts key data from business documents at scale, reducing manual errors and accelerating processing across financial and operational functions. Consistent application of these capabilities enables faster, more accurate, and more efficient supply chain performance across the organization. Start Your AI Transformation Journey with Ryder AI creates value when it becomes part of how supply chains operate day-to-day. When intelligence is embedded in transportation, warehousing, and fleet management, teams can respond faster, work more efficiently, and make better decisions with greater confidence. For many organizations, the challenge is not whether to use AI, but how to apply it in a way that delivers consistent results without adding unnecessary complexity. That requires an approach built around real operational needs, not isolated tools or one-off use cases. Ryder supports that approach by integrating AI directly into supply chain operations through RyderAI which connects data, systems, and workflows. The result is a more controlled, visible, and efficient operation that can scale with demand. Explore how Ryder can help you apply AI in supply chain operations to improve performance, reduce inefficiencies, and operate with greater clarity across your network.

title: How to Start Using Drones for Security Patrols
summary: Learn how to use drones for security patrols, connect alerts to aerial verification, evaluate vendors, and build a responsible plan with Aerodome DAS.
body_text: Drone security patrols work best when they start with a clear security problem: a large property that’s difficult to get eyes on, a slow verification process, a blind spot, or a response decision that needs better context. A practical launch plan should define where aerial visibility helps, confirm legal and site requirements, connect drone deployment to existing alerts, train the people who will use the system, and set rules for access, retention, authorized sharing, review, and escalation before the first flight. Aerodome Drone as Automated Security (DAS) is built for exactly that kind of program. Designed for commercial security teams that need rapid deployment and live incident context across large or hard-to-monitor properties, it uses a docked unmanned aerial vehicle that can be deployed remotely by a human operator after alarms, sensors, cameras, or other configured alert sources indicate an area that needs a closer look. It's worth distinguishing this from Drone as First Responder (DFR). DFR is a public safety model built around emergency calls, CAD events, and agency response , while Aerodome DAS is designed for private-sector asset protection, site security, and security-team response. The operating rules, deployment criteria, and public expectations are different — and that distinction shapes everything about how each program is built and run. Key Takeaways Start with the security problem, not the technology. Drone patrols add the most value when they're tied to a specific gap: a blind spot, slow alarm verification, a large property, or a response decision that needs better aerial context before personnel are deployed. Aerodome DAS is built for commercial security, not public safety response. It's designed for private-sector asset protection and site security and is distinct from Drone as First Responder (DFR), which is built around emergency calls and agency response. The operating rules, deployment criteria, and public expectations differ between the two. Human oversight is always part of the process. Aerodome DAS is not fully autonomous. A trained operator initiates and manages every deployment. The system provides live aerial visibility and context, but people make the response decisions. Drones work best as a connected layer, not a standalone tool. When integrated with existing alarms, fixed cameras, LPR, and SOC procedures, drones reduce guesswork from detection through verification to response. Operating in isolation just adds another screen to manage. Governance and clear rules are operational. Before launch, teams should define who can deploy, who can access footage, where drones may fly, how long footage is retained, and when public safety coordination is appropriate. A well-governed program is easier to use, audit, and defend. Where Drone Security Patrols Add Value A drone adds value when a better view changes the next decision. That may mean verifying an alarm before sending a guard, checking a far edge of a facility after hours, or giving a SOC enough context to decide whether to escalate an incident. Common environments include logistics yards, warehouses, industrial facilities, shopping centers, campuses, parking areas, loading docks, trailer lots, and fenced perimeters. These sites often have wide footprints, limited sightlines, changing activity patterns, or areas that take too long to reach on foot or by vehicle. Strong use cases include: Alarm verification: Give the SOC a live aerial view before dispatching a guard or escalating internally. On-demand after-hours perimeter checks: Inspect gates, yards, fence lines, access points, and remote corners without sending a person first. Loading dock and trailer lot visibility: Help security teams understand movement across a wide operating area. Parking area response: Give authorized stakeholders a better view of activity near vehicles, entrances, or gathering points. Blind spot inspection: Add mobile aerial visibility where fixed cameras cannot see enough. ‍ Drones provide visibility and context. They do not replace human judgment, site policy, or response personnel. How a Drone Security Patrol Response Works A responsible drone security patrol program connects an alert or operator request to a defined response process. The drone technology gives the team live aerial visibility, while trained people decide what happens next. A typical response looks like this: An alarm, sensor, camera alert, or operator request identifies an area that needs attention. A docked drone is deployed by or under the direction of a trained operator, according to the property’s operating rules and applicable requirements. The drone travels to the location and streams live video to authorized SOC users or stakeholders for the specific response. The team reviews the scene, using available visibility tools such as zoom or thermal where supported. Security leaders decide whether to send guards, notify management, document the event, or coordinate with public safety when appropriate. ‍ For current Aerodome DAS deployments, human oversight remains part of the process. The system supports remote deployment and operation, but it is not a fully autonomous patrol, autonomous alert response, or a system that makes security decisions on its own. When an alert requires drone response, a human operator remains responsible for initiating and managing the deployment. How to Start a Drone Security Patrol Program Start with the site, not the aircraft. The right plan makes drone deployment useful under pressure and defensible after the fact. A practical launch plan should: Define the operating problem. Identify the incidents, assets, hours, and zones where aerial visibility would change a response decision. Assess the site and airspace. Review property layout, lighting, launch locations, foot and vehicle traffic, nearby roads, night operations, FAA requirements, and any airspace restrictions. Connect existing systems. Decide how alarms, cameras, sensors, configured Flock integrations, SOC procedures, and escalation paths will trigger or inform a drone response. Set governance rules. Define who can deploy the drone, who can view or share live or recorded footage, where the drone may fly, how long footage is retained, and how incidents are reviewed and audited. Train and measure. Document procedures, train operators, and review performance against goals such as faster verification, fewer unnecessary guard dispatches, safer response decisions, better coverage, and clearer incident documentation. ‍ Do not assume beyond visual line of sight operations, flights over people, flights over active roadways or vehicles, or night flights are available without the required FAA review, waivers, or site approvals. Site conditions, FAA requirements, local rules, and any required approvals should be confirmed before launch. How Drones Fit with Guards, Alarms, and Fixed Cameras Drone security patrols are most useful as a connected layer in a broader security program. Guards provide judgment, presence, intervention, and incident handoff. Alarms detect activity, but they often lack the context needed to separate a false alarm from a real issue. Fixed cameras provide persistent coverage in known locations, but their field of view is limited. A drone adds mobile aerial verification. When an alert fires or a security operator needs a better view, the team can look across a larger area before deciding who needs to respond and how. This is where integration matters. A drone that operates apart from the rest of the security program creates another screen to watch and another process to manage. A drone connected to alerts, cameras, and SOC procedures can help the team move from detection to verification to response with less guesswork. What to Look for in a Drone Security Patrol Solution A drone security patrol solution should fit the property, the staffing model, and the rules that govern how it will be used. Price matters, but a lower hardware cost has limited value if the system cannot be deployed reliably, governed clearly, or used by the team responsible for response. Evaluate vendors against practical operating criteria: Docked readiness for rapid deployment across large or hard-to-monitor properties Remote operation with clear human controls Fit with existing cameras, alarms, sensors, SOC tools, and escalation procedures Live video quality and supported visibility options, including zoom, thermal, night, or low-light capabilities where appropriate Site planning support, operator training, and written operating procedures FAA and site-readiness guidance, including airspace, waiver, and flight restriction considerations Role-based access, retention settings, reviewability, and audit trails Support model for installation, maintenance, updates, and ongoing operations ‍ Pricing should be evaluated as total program cost. Include hardware, software, installation, maintenance, support, training, staffing, compliance work, coverage requirements, and the operational value of faster verification. A site-specific coverage and workflow discussion is usually more useful than a generic price estimate because every property has different constraints. How Aerodome Drone as Automated Security (DAS) Supports Commercial Security Aerodome Drone as Automated Security (DAS) helps commercial security teams see and assess a scene faster. It connects a docked drone to the alerts, people, and procedures that already shape property response. Aerodome DAS supports remote deployment and operation through authorized access from a laptop with an internet connection. A trained operator can use keyboard and mouse controls to pilot the drone and provide live visibility around the customer’s site. Where supported, teams can use enhanced views such as zoom and thermal to better understand what is happening before sending people into the field. Aerodome DAS can also work alongside other customer-configured Flock tools, including license plate reader (LPR) cameras, Audio Detection, and other alert sources. Those systems can surface a configured alert or location for review, while human operators remain responsible for deployment and response decisions. Flock is the connected safety platform behind the operation, not a substitute for the people accountable for safety. The goal is clearer context, faster verification, and better coordination across the teams already responsible for protecting the property. Responsible Deployment and Public Safety Coordination Drone programs earn trust through clear rules. Before launch, security leaders should be able to explain where drones may fly, what events justify deployment, who can access or share footage, how footage is retained, how reviews are audited, and when public safety coordination is appropriate. That clarity helps employees, tenants, visitors, and community stakeholders understand the purpose and limits of the program. It also gives security teams a consistent standard to follow during high-pressure incidents. Responsible deployment is not separate from operational performance. A program with defined access, retention, authorized sharing, review, and escalation rules is easier to use, audit, and explain. Flock’s broader approach to responsible technology is outlined in the Trust Center , including transparency, customer control, and accountability. Public-sector leaders who want to understand how emergency drone programs differ can also read Flock’s guide to public safety drone operations . Build a Site-specific Drone Security Patrol Plan The right drone security patrol plan is built around your property’s risks, constraints, and response model. It should answer practical questions before procurement: what your team needs to see faster, which alerts need verification, who makes response decisions, where drones may operate, and how footage should be accessed and reviewed. Flock can help security and operations leaders evaluate site layout, alert sources, approved operating areas, FAA and site requirements, governance expectations, and how Aerodome Drone as Automated Security (DAS) could fit existing operations. Request a demo to talk through a responsible drone security patrol plan for your property. FAQs What Are Drone Security Patrols? Drone security patrols use an unmanned aerial vehicle to provide mobile aerial visibility over a defined property or approved operating area. They help security teams verify alerts, inspect hard-to-monitor areas, and make better response decisions. How Do Drone Security Patrols Work with Existing Cameras, Alarms, and Sensors? Existing systems surface alerts or locations for review. A drone can then provide live aerial context so authorized SOC users or stakeholders can decide whether to send guards, escalate internally, document the incident, or coordinate with public safety. How Are Drone Security Patrols Different From Drone as First Responder? Drone security patrols are private-sector security operations for commercial properties. Drone as First Responder is a public safety response model built around emergency calls, CAD events, or agency alerts. Aerodome DAS is designed for commercial asset protection and site security, while DFR is designed for public agencies. Can Drone Security Patrols Replace Guards or Fixed Cameras? They should be treated as a supplement, not a blanket replacement. Guards provide judgment and physical presence, fixed cameras provide persistent coverage in defined areas, and drones add mobile aerial verification across areas that are difficult to monitor or reach quickly. What Does Drone Security Patrol Pricing Depend On? Pricing depends on the size and layout of the property, launch locations, coverage requirements, hardware, software, installation, maintenance, support, training, staffing, and any compliance or waiver needs. A site-specific assessment is the best way to understand cost and program design. Is Aerodome DAS Fully Autonomous? No. Current Aerodome DAS capabilities are not fully autonomous patrol or autonomous alert response. The system supports remote deployment and operation, and a human operator remains part of the decision loop. title: Watch: Introducing the L.B. Foster 320' Rail Consist
summary: L.B. Foster is redefining rail delivery with the successful development and first-ever delivery of 320-foot rail to Lake State Railway in Michigan.
body_text: Transported using a five-car consist, this innovative rail solution eliminates the need for field welding while offering greater installation flexibility and significant cost savings. Unlike traditional 80' rail or continuous welded rail, the 320' can move in manifest freight traffic - delivering efficiency without the need for dedicated trains. The 320' rail represents a smarter, more durable approach to modern rail construction. Learn how L.B. Foster continues to advance rail performance through innovation. Learn more: https://lbfoster.com/rail.

title: Legal answering service: How law firms stop losing calls
summary: See what a legal answering service covers, how AI-based intake differs from live agents, and what to check before choosing one.
body_text: Pick up every client call, even when the whole team is in depositions, court, or back-to-back meetings. A prospective client calls your firm, gets voicemail, and hangs up. Thirty seconds later, they’re dialing the next practice on their search results page. That office answers, and you lose a client you never knew you had. This happens more often than most firms want to admit. Attorneys are in court. Paralegals are on other lines. Front-desk staff step away for lunch. Every gap in coverage is a gap a competitor is happy to fill. Closing that gap doesn’t require a bigger front desk or a paralegal glued to the phone. A legal answering service built for law firms catches the calls your team can’t. This guide breaks down what these services cover, how AI-based intake compares with a live-agent model, and what to check before you choose one. Key takeaways A legal answering service covers client intake calls, scheduling, and after-hours coverage when staff can’t get to the phone AI-based intake differs from live-agent services in consistency, cost, and integration with case tools Evaluate options on intake accuracy, confidentiality handling, and consistency across every call RingCentral AI Receptionist extends call handling into legal intake without adding headcount Why law firms miss more calls than they realize Attorneys and staff can’t sit by the phone. They’re in court, in depositions, or in back-to-back client meetings, and that’s exactly when a new caller decides whether your firm is worth waiting for. The data on this is worse than most firms assume. Clio’s 2024 Legal Trends Report found that only 40% of firms answered secret-shopper calls, down from 56% in 2019, and 48% of firms were essentially unreachable by phone. That means more than half of prospective clients calling a law firm today hit voicemail, get a busy signal, or receive no answer at all. Since each one of those callers is also calling other firms, whoever answers first usually gets the case. Missed calls don’t just cost new business. Existing clients calling with urgent updates, document requests, or case questions expect a quick response too. A firm that can’t answer consistently signals disorganization precisely when clients need reassurance. Think about what a caller does after voicemail picks up. Most won’t leave a message and wait for a callback. They go back to their search results, find another firm, and dial that number instead. The whole decision takes less than a minute. Part of the problem is timing. A three-attorney firm might have each partner unavailable for hours at a time, and front-desk staff can’t cover every line during lunch, sick days, or vacations. The fix isn’t hiring more intake specialists for a call volume that spikes unpredictably. It’s making sure every call gets handled the moment it comes in, whether through a dedicated legal virtual receptionist or an automated system built to capture new business. What a legal answering service covers A legal answering service exists to make sure incoming calls get handled, not just recorded. That distinction matters more than firms realize. At the core, these services answer and triage intake calls for lead capture. A new client calls with a personal injury question, an estate planning issue, or a custody dispute, and the law firm answering service gathers the basics: name, contact information, and the nature of the case. That information gets routed to the right attorney or paralegal instead of sitting in a voicemail inbox. Scheduling is the second piece. An effective answering service books consultations directly, without a staff member picking up the phone to coordinate calendars. The caller gets a confirmed time before they hang up, which matters when they’re comparing your firm against a handful of others. After-hours and overflow coverage rounds it out. A car accident doesn’t happen during business hours, and a caller in that situation who reaches a generic voicemail box will typically move on rather than leave a message. Coverage outside the 9-to-5 window closes that gap. With the right AI-based answering service , firms can now handle all three of these functions automatically. Live-agent services vs. AI-based intake Traditional legal intake services staff call centers with people trained on general scripts. They’re reachable, but the person answering usually doesn’t know your practice areas in depth, and quality varies by who’s on shift that day. An AI-based intake process works differently. Instead of routing to a person relying on static prompts, the system answers directly and handles routing or scheduling based on what the caller actually says. There’s no hold time waiting for an available agent, and the experience doesn’t change depending on time of day or call volume. The trade-offs come down to consistency, cost, and how well the service connects to the tools a firm already uses. Live-agent services charge per call or per minute, which adds up fast during busy periods. AI-based interactive voice response (AI IVR) tends to scale more predictably. Traditional menu-driven phone systems sit in between, routing calls but failing to hold actual conversations with callers. What to look for when evaluating a legal answering service Not every answering service for lawyers handles legal calls the same way, and the wrong choice can cost you clients instead of securing them. Intake accuracy. Does the service capture the details that matter for your practice areas and initial lead qualification, including the names and data required for conflict checks? A family law intake needs different information than a personal injury intake, and a generic script won’t ask the right follow-up questions. Ask potential vendors how their system adapts to different case types before you sign a contract. Confidentiality. Callers share sensitive details in the first 30 seconds of an intake call, including medical information, financial details, and family circumstances. You need a clear answer on how that information, including call recordings and transcripts, gets handled, stored, and passed along to your team. If a vendor can’t explain their process in plain terms, that’s a red flag. Consistency across every caller. A service that performs well at 2 PM but drops the ball at 2 AM isn’t solving your problem. Ask for performance data across different times of day, not just a demo during business hours. Fit with your existing systems. If the service can’t pass intake details into your case management system without manual re-entry, someone on your team is doing double work. The right fit reduces friction for your staff, not just for callers. Firms exploring AI tools built for smaller teams should weigh setup time against what they’re already paying for coverage gaps. Pricing structure. Per-call or per-minute billing sounds simple until call volume spikes during a marketing push or a high-profile case brings in a wave of inquiries. Understand how costs scale before volume grows, not after the first invoice arrives. A pilot run. Route a subset of your intake line to the new service for a few weeks and compare the details captured against what your staff would have gathered on the same calls. That comparison tells you more than any vendor pitch. How RingCentral AI Receptionist handles this for law firms Firms need every call answered professionally, but staffing a dedicated intake desk around the clock isn’t realistic for most. Hiring overnight or weekend coverage for occasional call volume rarely pencils out. RingCentral’s AI Receptionist (AIR) answers incoming calls automatically, before a human ever joins the line. It captures leads and routes callers based on what they say they need, whether they want to open a new case, ask a question as an existing client, or speak directly with an attorney. AIR also supports appointment scheduling directly during the call. A prospective client calling about a car accident can get a consultation booked without waiting for a callback, securing the opportunity right then and there. For solo attorneys or firms handling overflow during trial prep or after hours, AIR keeps every inquiry moving forward. It manages intake naturally, avoiding the friction of traditional button-based menus. Finally, AIR is compliant with multiple privacy and security regulations, including the Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard (PCI DSS), the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA), and the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). It’s also SOC 2 certified, so your clients’ personal data isn’t at risk when the AI Receptionist picks up the phone. Stop letting a missed call become a lost client A missed call isn’t a small operational gap. It’s a prospective client choosing a different firm or an existing client losing confidence in yours. Consistent, professional call handling protects both sides of that equation: new intake and the trust your current clients already have. Whether you choose a live-agent service or an AI-based system, the standard is the same: every call gets answered, every time, regardless of how busy your team gets. If your firm is still relying on voicemail during busy stretches, it’s worth seeing how RingCentral AIR can handle legal intake calls around the clock. FAQs about legal answering services What does a legal answering service do? A legal answering service answers incoming calls for a law firm, captures intake details from new clients, and schedules consultations. Many also provide after-hours and overflow coverage so callers always reach a professional response instead of an unanswered line. Is an AI legal answering service confidential? How caller information is handled varies by provider, and firms should confirm data handling and storage practices directly before choosing a service. Look for compliance with regulations like the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), the Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard (PCI DSS), and the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA), as well as SOC 2. Can a legal answering service schedule consultations directly? Yes. Many attorney answering services, including AI-based intake tools, can handle administrative tasks like booking consultations during the call instead of routing the caller to voicemail or a callback queue. This gets a confirmed appointment on the calendar before the caller hangs up. How is an AI answering service different from a traditional legal call center? A traditional call center employs people trained on general intake scripts, and quality can vary by who’s on shift. An AI-based service answers directly and routes or schedules based on what the caller says, without hold times, and performs the same way regardless of call volume or time of day. Originally published Jul 30, 2026

title: Solstice Advanced Materials To Invest Over $220 Million To Expand Ballistic Fiber Manufacturing In Chesterfield County, Virginia
body_text: Expansion to strengthen U.S. manufacturing of defense-critical materials, enhance innovation and create 100 full-time high-tech jobs MORRIS PLAINS, N.J., January 13, 2026 – Solstice Advanced Materials (NASDAQ: SOLS), a global leader in high-performance specialty materials, today announced plans to invest more than $220 million in multiple projects to expand production at its existing ballistic fiber manufacturing facility in Colonial Heights, Chesterfield County, Virginia, which is also expected to create 100 new full-time jobs in the region by 2029. The Colonial Heights facility has been a cornerstone of U.S. defense supply chains for over two decades, producing Spectra® fiber and composite materials used in helmets, vests, vehicle armor and naval applications, along with an array of industrial applications. Through its investment, Solstice will enhance its facility with new fiber spinning, composite coating and analytical capabilities, creating one of the most sophisticated ballistic materials production hubs in North America. Construction and equipment installation are expected to occur between 2025 and 2029, with operational benefits expected to ramp through the projected completion date of Sept. 30, 2030. “This investment underscores Solstice’s commitment to maintaining technology leadership in high-performance protective materials, strengthening U.S.-based manufacturing and enhancing supply chain resiliency for defense-critical materials,” said David Sewell, President and CEO of Solstice Advanced Materials. “Our advanced fibers and composites deliver critical protection across defense, law enforcement and industrial applications – all of which represent significant growth markets for Solstice.” “Solstice Advanced Materials’ expansion in Chesterfield underscores Virginia’s leadership in the advanced manufacturing and materials industry,” said Governor Glenn Youngkin. “Their ballistic fibers help protect those who protect us, and this growth reflects the strength of the Commonwealth’s talent. Partnerships like this will ensure Virginia remains the best place to build and innovate.” “Solstice’s commitment to Chesterfield is a win for the Commonwealth and for our advanced manufacturing ecosystem,” said Secretary of Commerce and Trade Juan Pablo Segura. “Virginia’s reliable infrastructure, pro-business climate, and world‑class workforce give innovators the confidence to scale critical technologies right here at home.” The expansion will increase capacity for Spectra® and Spectra Shield® technologies, featuring ultra-high molecular weight polyethylene (UHMWPE) fibers that are up to 15 times stronger than steel and 65% lighter than aramid fabrics. The Colonial Heights facility’s state-of-the-art R&D and prototyping capabilities – spanning fiber spinning, ballistic testing and composite fabrication – enable Solstice to accelerate innovation cycles and deliver mission-critical advancements such as next-generation lightweight armor systems and advanced soldier protection solutions. The project also supports the U.S. military’s strategic objective to maintain and expand domestic production of advanced ballistic materials amid rising global competition. The Virginia Economic Development Partnership (VEDP), in coordination with Chesterfield County, supported the project through the Virginia Investment Performance (VIP) Grant, which provides consultative services and funding to companies creating new jobs in order to support employee recruitment and training activities. Additionally, Governor Glenn Youngkin approved a $1.5 million grant from the Commonwealth’s Opportunity Fund and a $2 million performance-based Virginia Investment Performance (VIP) Grant to assist Chesterfield County with the project and encourage continued capital investment by existing Virginia companies. “This expansion reflects our long-term confidence in the Commonwealth of Virginia and our commitment to advancing America’s defense industrial base,” said Lawrence Kast, Senior Vice President, Global Government Relations, Solstice Advanced Materials. “We’re grateful for the collaborative support from state and local leaders, whose partnership ensures that the critical materials needed for national defense continue to be produced here in the United States.” About Solstice Advanced Materials Solstice Advanced Materials is a leading global specialty materials company that advances science for smarter outcomes. Solstice offers high-performance solutions that enable critical industries and applications, including refrigerants, semiconductor manufacturing, data center, cooling, nuclear power, protective fibers, healthcare packaging and more. Solstice is recognized for developing next-generation materials through some of the industry's most renowned brands such as Solstice®, Genetron®, Aclar®, Spectra®, Fluka™ and Hydranal™. Partnering with over 3,000 customers across more than 120 countries and territories and supported by a robust portfolio of over 5,700 patents, Solstice’s approximately 4,000 employees worldwide drive innovation in materials science. For more information, visit www.Solstice.com . title: Noble Corporation PLC Completes Sale Of Five Jackups To Borr Drilling
summary: HOUSTON, Jan. 28, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Noble Corporation plc (NYSE: NE, "Noble", or the "Company") today announced that it has completed the
body_text: HOUSTON, Jan. 28, 2026 /PRNewswire/ — Noble Corporation plc (NYSE: NE, “Noble”, or the “Company”) today announced that it has completed the sale of five jackup rigs to Borr Drilling Limited (NYSE: BORR, “Borr”) for $360 million. The Company generated approximately $210 million in cash plus $150 million in seller notes from the sale of the Noble Tom Prosser, Noble Mick O’Brien, Noble Regina Allen, Noble Resilient and Noble Resolute. Noble intends to operate two rigs – Noble Mick O’Brien and Noble Resolute – under a bareboat charter agreement with Borr until December 2026, as well as the Noble Resilient through the remainder of its current contract term (including exercise of any customer options). For additional information, visit www.noblecorp.com or e-mail investors@noblecorp.com . About Noble Corporation plc Noble is a leading offshore drilling contractor for the oil and gas industry. The Company owns and operates one of the most modern, versatile, and technically advanced fleets in the offshore drilling industry. Noble and its predecessors have been engaged in the contract drilling of oil and gas wells since 1921. Noble performs, through its subsidiaries, contract drilling services with a fleet of offshore drilling units focused largely on ultra-deepwater and high specification jackup drilling opportunities in both established and emerging regions worldwide. Additional information on Noble is available at www.noblecorp.com .
